claims.text: Combining machine-learned interatomic potentials with replica exchange or metadynamics will enable free-energy integration for both solid and liquid phases near melting.
The proposed method will retain high fidelity for vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration entropy contributions.
The proposed method will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
A limited set of targeted ab initio molecular-dynamics trajectories near the melting point is sufficient to train the required potential.
Thermodynamic integration driven by the trained potential can rigorously account for vibrational spectra, anharmonic fluctuations, and electron–vibration coupling.
The trained interatomic potential will accurately preserve local chemical ordering in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The trained potential will reproduce vibrational and anharmonic behavior in both solid and liquid phases.
The ML potential approximates the full ab initio energy landscape while greatly reducing the cost per simulation step.
Replica exchange or metadynamics will overcome relevant energy barriers and ensure complete phase-space exploration.
The method is applicable to elemental materials, binary alloys, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The method will perform as predicted at temperatures within approximately 10% of the melting temperature.
The predicted performance is restricted to compositions represented in the ML training set.
Phase free-energy differences and derived melting temperatures will agree with explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results to within approximately 5%.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational cost by a factor of 5–10 relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed workflow will have superior throughput to TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy integration and TOR-TILD are accurate for elemental and binary systems.
TOR-TILD becomes computationally prohibitive for high-entropy alloys.
Sparse training data for rare events or extreme compositional complexity may reduce the method's reliability.
A deviation greater than 5% in phase free-energy differences relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics is a falsifying result.
